candidateRows: Hand copying propagated inherited mistakes while adding new ones, producing increasingly divergent textual forms.
This transmission mechanism supplies the causal foundation for Ehrman's claim that surviving copies can differ from the authors' wording.
Ehrman explains how handwritten copies generated mistakes, preserved predecessors' errors, and sometimes introduced uncertain attempted corrections.
The long undocumented gap between the originals and surviving manuscripts prevents knowledge of changes made during early copying stages.
The absence of originals and early intermediary copies directly supports the con position that autographic certainty cannot be achieved.
Using Mark and P45, Ehrman argues that centuries and many unknown copying stages separate originals from the earliest useful surviving witnesses.
The abundance of New Testament manuscripts does not solve the problem because most witnesses are late and depend on unknown earlier exemplars.
This argument answers the evidentiary force of manuscript abundance by emphasizing the lateness and fragmentary nature of early witnesses.
Ehrman concedes that New Testament copies are numerous, then contrasts that abundance with scant early fragments and predominantly medieval manuscripts.
Surviving manuscripts contain more textual differences than the New Testament contains words, while earlier unobserved differences remain unknowable.
The scale of observed variation and uncertainty about lost early variants materially supports doubt about complete recovery of original wording.
Ehrman traces variant counting from John Mill's edition to modern estimates and stresses that no complete count or early total is available.
Most manuscript variants are insignificant accidental errors that trained critics can usually identify and correct.
The concession sharply limits the significance of raw variant totals and defines which remaining variants must carry Ehrman's uncertainty argument.
Ehrman distinguishes ordinary misspellings, omissions, duplications, and similar copying slips from consequential variants, noting their usual detectability.
The earliest Christian copyists were probably less trained than later scribes, so substantial early errors may predate all surviving evidence.
This inference targets the inaccessible period closest to the originals and explains why later manuscript comparison cannot guarantee autographic recovery.
Ehrman contrasts trained medieval and fourth-century scribes with less capable earlier copyists, while acknowledging that neither debater can know the lost record.
The available evidence cannot establish complete textual reliability because some original readings remain disputed or permanently unknowable.
This conclusion directly answers the debate motion and states the con side's ultimate inference from lost witnesses and consequential variants.
Ehrman concludes that continuing scholarly disputes and irrecoverable readings make categorical reliability unavailable and that the uncertainty matters.
Some intentional or consequential variants alter prominent passages and doctrinally significant wording despite the insignificance of most variants.
Concrete disputed passages show why the residual class of meaningful variants matters to trust even after conceding that most differences are trivial.
Ehrman surveys disputed wording concerning the Trinity, Jesus' divinity, Luke's atonement theology, the adulterous woman, Mark's ending, and Jesus' prayer.
Some intentional textual changes affect important passages, leaving no way to know the original wording in every disputed place.
This conclusion directly supports the negative position by connecting consequential variants and unresolved passages to the limits of textual recovery.
After presenting disputed sayings and narrative passages, Ehrman concludes that meaningful variants remain and that some original readings cannot be known.
The central dispute concerns the significance of textual variants and whether the original wording can be recovered with relative confidence.
The move states Wallace's governing thesis and isolates the two questions that directly determine his answer to the debate motion.
Ehrman's claim that consequential variants make the original wording unknowable in some places.
Following extensive concessions about variants and disputed passages, Wallace distinguishes their existence from their significance and recoverability.
Scribal alteration did not erase the original wording because identifying corruption itself presupposes recoverable earlier readings among the manuscripts.
This argument directly answers the possibility that early intentional alteration permanently removed the original text from the surviving tradition.
Ehrman's contention that changes before the earliest surviving copies may have left no recoverable evidence.
Wallace argues that scholarly detection of Orthodox and unorthodox tampering depends on comparing altered readings with identifiable prior wording.
The large variant count results from an exceptionally large witness base, whose manuscripts, translations, and patristic citations improve reconstruction.
The argument reverses the inference from numerous variants by treating them as a consequence of abundant independent evidence for reconstructing the text.
Ehrman's use of the enormous number of manuscript differences as grounds for doubting textual reliability.
Wallace defines variants, relates their number to manuscript abundance, and adds ancient translations and church-father citations as further witnesses.
Compared with classical literature, the New Testament has unusually early and abundant witnesses, while later copies add relatively little material.
The comparison supplies an external benchmark for judging whether the age, quantity, and stability of the manuscript tradition permit responsible recovery.
The skeptical inference that late surviving manuscripts make the New Testament no more recoverable than other ancient works.
Wallace contrasts early New Testament witnesses and limited later expansion with sparse, late, incomplete, and gap-filled classical manuscript traditions.
The New Testament's exceptional manuscript attestation makes radical doubt inconsistent with ordinary confidence in the rest of ancient history.
This synthesis directly links abundant variants and manuscripts to a favorable recovery claim while challenging the consistency of broader historical skepticism.
Ehrman's conclusion that the surviving evidence cannot establish a sufficiently reliable original New Testament text.
Wallace characterizes the manuscript problem as abundance rather than scarcity and argues that equivalent skepticism would undermine ancient history generally.
Most textual variants make virtually no difference because they involve spelling, word order, articles, or other forms that translate identically.
The move addresses significance rather than raw quantity, showing why a large numerical total need not imply widespread uncertainty about textual meaning.
Ehrman's reliance on the scale of manuscript variation to argue that textual differences materially impair trust.
Wallace explains that Greek permits numerous formally different constructions with unchanged meaning, making many counted variants substantively trivial.
Fewer than one percent of variants are both meaningful and viable, though hundreds of genuinely disputed passages still affect interpretation.
The argument quantifies the consequential subset while conceding unresolved cases, supporting relative confidence without claiming complete textual certainty.
Ehrman's examples of disputed and consequential readings offered to show that textual changes seriously matter.
Using disputed readings in Mark and Revelation, Wallace acknowledges meaningful cases but places them within a small viable subset of all variants.
No viable textual variant has been shown to overturn an essential Christian belief, even though individual passages may remain disputed.
The move bears on the practical trustworthiness of the text by separating local uncertainty from instability in core theological claims.
The suggestion that important intentional changes and disputed passages may compromise consequential Christian claims.
Wallace turns from the frequency of meaningful variants to their doctrinal impact and invokes common ground about essential beliefs.
New Testament transmission is unlike a telephone game because multiple written lines, early commentators, and continued access to earlier copies preserve checks.
The move directly explains why missing originals and intermediate copies do not entail uncontrolled linear corruption or prevent reconstruction of earlier wording.
Ehrman's emphasis that the originals and the earliest generations of copies no longer survive for direct comparison.
Wallace argues that written, branching transmission permits comparison across scribes and patristic testimony, while earlier exemplars could remain available.
The standard critical Greek text indicates that the autographic wording survives among the manuscript readings in virtually every disputed place.
This converts the critical edition's treatment of conjectural readings into direct support for the claim that the original wording remains recoverable from extant witnesses.
Ehrman's contention that early corruption prevents confidence that surviving readings preserve the autographic wording.

Wallace describes the critical text and its apparatus, contrasts many listed variants with very few proposed conjectures, and argues that an original reading is ordinarily represented among the available alternatives.
New Testament scholarship, including Ehrman's own authorship arguments, routinely presupposes reliable knowledge of the wording in nearly every relevant passage.
The move alleges a practical inconsistency between denying recoverability and conducting detailed scholarship that depends on stable wording across multiple New Testament books.
Ehrman's denial that scholars can know whether the reconstructed text corresponds to the authors' original wording.
Wallace invokes the scholarly consensus and then uses Ehrman's vocabulary-based analysis of disputed Pauline letters as an example of research that requires dependable access to the relevant wording.
Wallace's presentation does not supply evidence establishing that surviving witnesses preserve the original wording, and Ehrman's older statements do not resolve that problem.
This identifies the con side's governing objection to Wallace's case: evidence from surviving witnesses cannot by itself establish what happened before those witnesses existed.
Wallace's appeal to Ehrman's earlier publications as evidence that even Ehrman presupposes recovery of the original text.

Ehrman notes substantial agreement but says Wallace has not reached the central epistemic issue, rejects reliance on older books because his view changed, and renews the demand for supporting evidence.
The small proportion of meaningful and viable surviving variants does not address potentially significant changes introduced before the earliest surviving manuscripts.
It distinguishes the measurable variation in extant evidence from the unobservable transmission period, blocking a principal quantitative argument for confidence in the text.
Wallace's argument that only a very small percentage of the numerous surviving variants are both meaningful and viable.
Ehrman provisionally accepts Wallace's percentage but argues that it concerns only surviving variants, then asks how anyone could count omissions, editions, or alterations predating extant witnesses.
A textual difference can be historically significant even when it changes no essential Christian doctrine, so doctrinal stability is not an adequate measure of textual significance.
This rebuts a major trust argument by separating theological consequences from historical and textual importance, preserving the relevance of substantial variants.
Wallace's reassurance that no essential Christian belief is affected by any viable textual variant in the manuscripts.
Ehrman accepts that variants may leave doctrine unchanged but uses the hypothetical disappearance of several whole books to show that losses can remain extremely important without altering a creed.
Confidence in the New Testament requires an evidential basis for believing that the earliest surviving copies descend from accurate rather than seriously altered predecessors.
The move states the core con challenge linking unavailable pre-survival transmission evidence directly to whether the text can responsibly be trusted.
Wallace's conclusion that the original New Testament wording is recoverable with relative confidence from the accumulated evidence.

Ehrman asks how Wallace knows significant alteration did not occur before extant witnesses, sharpens the issue to whether early copies had accurate exemplars, and connects inability to answer with trust.
Early circulation, repeated copying, independent versions, and patristic witnesses provide cumulative probabilistic evidence against a sparse and unrecoverable initial transmission.
This supplies Wallace's principal evidential response to the missing-first-copies objection by arguing that early branching created multiple independent lines of textual control.
Ehrman's claim that nothing establishes whether the first copies were accurate or how much alteration preceded surviving manuscripts.

Wallace cites circulation of Pauline letters, use of Mark by Matthew and Luke, repeated reading and copying, comparison with classical works, early versions, and patristic material as converging evidence.

Although hard proof about the earliest copies is unavailable, substantial indirect evidence makes it probable that the extant text preserves what the New Testament authors wrote in essential respects.
The move expressly defines the affirmative standard as warranted probability rather than certainty and applies it directly to essential textual recoverability.
Ehrman's repeated demand for hard evidence proving that pre-survival copies were accurate and free from significant alteration.

Wallace concedes that neither side possesses hard evidence about the missing period but maintains that the accumulated indirect evidence supports confidence in essential continuity with the authors' writings.
Contemporary textual criticism can reconstruct the earliest text from which surviving witnesses descend without establishing that this reconstructed initial text is the author's original.
This draws the decisive con distinction between attainable reconstruction and autographic identification, directly limiting what textual criticism can warrant about the motion.
Wallace's claim that most scholars believe the original New Testament wording has been substantially recovered.
Ehrman says major scholarly centers avoid the language of original text and instead reconstruct the ancestral text behind surviving witnesses, whose identity with the autograph remains unknown.
The relevant scholarly consensus is that the New Testament has been largely recovered in essentials, even if textual critics qualify the terminology used for the original text.
This preserves the affirmative conclusion by distinguishing terminological caution among specialist textual critics from the broader scholarly practice of relying on an essentially recovered text.
Ehrman's argument that specialists' abandonment of the term original text undermines Wallace's appeal to scholarly consensus.

Wallace clarifies that his claim concerned New Testament scholars rather than every textual critic, appeals to ordinary scholarly analysis as evidence, and asserts recovery in essentials even for corrupt witnesses.
The initial text is not necessarily the original text, and the terminology changed because critics cannot establish that they have reached the original.
The distinction directly supports the con position that reconstructing an earliest attainable text does not establish recovery of the autograph.
Wallace's claim that current textual critics still seek and effectively mean the original text despite altered terminology.
During a direct exchange about disciplinary terminology, Ehrman argues that institutions abandoned the phrase original text because the initial text may only approximate it.
Leading textual-criticism figures use initial-text terminology while still treating it as equivalent to what was formerly called the original text.
This challenges the con side's inference from changed terminology and supports continuity between current reconstruction goals and recovery of the original.
Ehrman's contention that scholars adopted initial-text language precisely because the original text cannot be recovered.
Wallace answers the terminology argument by invoking prominent figures who avoid the older phrase yet allegedly retain the same substantive reconstruction objective.
Disagreements among the Synoptic Gospels may reflect Matthew and Luke having different textual forms of Mark before them.
The proposal supplies a concrete mechanism by which copying variation could already affect source texts used by New Testament authors.
The audience question asking how substantial verbal agreement among the Synoptics fits claims of early uncontrolled copying.
Answering a Synoptic Problem question, Ehrman emphasizes both agreement and disagreement and endorses the view that Matthew and Luke used differing forms of Mark.
Redactional analysis can test for a corrupted intermediate Mark, and the lack of changes contrary to Matthew's tendencies weighs against scribal corruption before him.
The proposed method and reported negative finding answer a concrete historical claim that textual corruption explains Synoptic differences.
Ehrman's proposal that Matthew and Luke may have possessed different, non-pristine textual forms of the Gospel of Mark.
Wallace proposes isolating readings that conflict with Matthew's redactional habits, then reports finding none and attributes the changes to Matthew's purposes instead.
Very early, nearly identical copies close to Mark's composition would be strong evidence of trustworthiness, but no such evidence survives.
It specifies the con side's evidentiary threshold and emphasizes that the surviving manuscript record lacks the kind of early control needed to meet it.
The audience request for evidence short of the autographs that would convince Ehrman the transmitted text is trustworthy.
Ehrman imagines multiple copies produced within a week of Mark and agreeing almost completely, calling that good evidence while stressing its absence.
Having more New Testament manuscripts than classical works makes reconstruction comparatively easier, but does not prove recovery of the original New Testament.
This directly rebuts a principal comparative-manuscript argument by separating relative evidentiary abundance from successful recovery of an autograph.
Wallace's manuscript-abundance comparison and the audience challenge about applying Ehrman's evidentiary standard to classical literature.
Ehrman concedes the New Testament's numerical manuscript advantage, argues classical texts can be even harder to reconstruct, and notes intentional Christian scribal changes.
The surviving text is probably related to what Mark wrote, but its unknown degree of difference and substantial variants prevent confident claims of trustworthiness.
The argument states the con position at the motion level: historical probability permits broad continuity but not sufficient knowledge to warrant textual trust.
Opening his conclusion, Ehrman rejects complete skepticism but stresses unknown divergence, invokes the longer form of Acts, and highlights admitted unresolved places.
Because the advocate of textual trust bears the burden of proof, uncertainty about the earliest untrained copyists and their exemplars defeats warranted confidence.
It assigns the decisive burden on the motion and ties the missing first two centuries of transmission directly to failure to establish trust.
Wallace's overall case that the available manuscript tradition provides sufficient grounds to trust the recovered New Testament text.
Ehrman compares trusting the text to sending passengers over a bridge, arguing that unknown early scribal competence and exemplar quality leave the required safety unproved.
Demanding certainty unavailable for any ancient text would erase historical knowledge; a moderate probabilistic standard permits responsible textual confidence.
This supplies the pro side's governing epistemic standard and argues that the con side's demanded threshold would undermine ancient history generally.
Ehrman's bridge analogy and argument that the proponent of trust must overcome uncertainty about the earliest transmission.
Wallace reframes everyone as traveling the same historical mountain road and argues for probability rather than absolute certainty or radical skepticism.
Ehrman's own scholarship presupposes sufficiently stable wording of authentic New Testament writings, undermining his portrayal of Wallace's view as certainty.
The internal-consistency challenge argues that ordinary New Testament scholarship itself depends on recoverability adequate for meaningful textual judgments.
Ehrman's repeated emphasis that the original wording remains unknown and Wallace's position improperly claims certainty.
Wallace accepts probabilistic historical judgment, denies claiming absolute certainty, and argues that Ehrman's analyses of Pauline vocabulary already assume a substantially known text.
